slides.title: Session outline: simple linear regression
paragraphs: The session develops simple linear regression, which describes how the mean of one variable changes with another, and then correlation, which measures how strongly two variables move together. The readings are Glantz pages 143 to 161, 164 to 169 and 177 to 178.

The outline runs from the idea of a population line of means, through estimating that line from a sample by least squares, to the spread of points about the line and the standard errors of the intercept and slope. Hypothesis tests and confidence intervals for the slope, the intercept, the line of means and a single new observation follow.
The final parts compare two regression lines, define the Pearson correlation coefficient and its t test, and show the R function lm() that produces the same quantities from data.

slides.title: Discussion outline: lm(), cor() and examples
paragraphs: The discussion section repeats the lecture topics in R. Linear regression is run with the lm() function, and correlation is computed with the cor() function.
Each R result corresponds to a quantity that can also be calculated by hand: the intercept, the slope, their standard errors, the residual standard error, and the correlation coefficient.
The examples that follow are the Plutonian height and weight data and the two lm() exercises at the end of the session.

slides.title: Where regression fits among the course methods
paragraphs: The summary table sorts statistical methods by the scale of measurement and the type of experiment. The circled methods are those already covered: the unpaired t test, analysis of variance, the z test, chi-square contingency tables, and relative risk or odds ratios.
The highlighted column is association between two variables. For interval data drawn from Normal populations, the methods are linear regression and the Pearson product-moment correlation.

Regression and correlation differ from the earlier tests because each subject supplies a pair of measurements. The question is not whether group means differ but whether, and how strongly, one measured variable changes with another.

slides.title: The Martian population: weight rises with height
paragraphs: The example population is 200 Martians. Height x is Normal with mean 40 cm and SD 5 cm, and weight y is Normal with mean 12 g and SD 2.5 g.
Describing each variable separately misses the relationship between them. In the scatter of the whole population, the mean weight of Martians at each height increases as height increases.

The population is built to meet the regression assumptions. The weights at any given height are Normal, the mean weight rises linearly with height, and the spread of weights is the same at every height. The population values are \(\alpha=-8\) g, \(\beta=0.5\) g/cm and \(\sigma_{y|x}=1\) g.
slides.symbols: \(X\) (height, cm), \(Y\) (weight, g), \(N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) (Normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\)).

slides.title: The line of means and the constant spread about it
paragraphs: The independent variable x is height and the dependent variable y is weight. At every fixed x, the population of y values has its own mean, written \(\mu_{y|x}\). The line joining these means is the line of means, \(\mu_{y|x}=\alpha+\beta x\).

The weights at a given height are Normally distributed about that mean with standard deviation \(\sigma_{y|x}\). The two Normal curves drawn on the line have the same width, which shows that \(\sigma_{y|x}\) is constant along the line.

For the Martians the line of means is \(\mu_{y|x}=-8\text{ g}+(0.5\text{ g/cm})x\) and \(\sigma_{y|x}=1\) g. A Martian 40 cm tall therefore has a mean weight of \(-8+0.5(40)=12\) g, and individual weights at that height scatter about 12 g with an SD of 1 g.
slides.symbols: \(\mu_{y|x}\) (population mean of y at a given x), \(\alpha\) (intercept of the line of means), \(\beta\) (slope of the line of means), \(\sigma_{y|x}\) (population SD of y about the line).

slides.title: Three assumptions for the population
paragraphs: The first assumption is linearity: the mean of the dependent variable at a given value of the independent variable increases or decreases linearly as the independent variable increases, \(\mu_{y|x}=\alpha+\beta x\).
The second assumption is Normality: for any given value of the independent variable, the possible values of the dependent variable are Normally distributed about \(\mu_{y|x}\).

The third assumption is constant spread: the standard deviation of the dependent variable about its mean, \(\sigma_{y|x}\), is the same for every value of the independent variable. The assumptions concern y at each fixed x; no Normal distribution is required for x itself.
slides.symbols: \(\mu_{y|x}\) (mean of y at x), \(\alpha,\beta\) (population intercept and slope), \(\sigma_{y|x}\) (SD of y about the line of means).

slides.title: Estimating the trend from a sample
paragraphs: In practice the whole population is not available. An investigator draws a random sample, here 10 Martians, shown as filled points among the 200 members of the population.
The population line of means is fixed but unknown. The sample has to be used to estimate its intercept \(\alpha\) and slope \(\beta\).

A different random sample of 10 Martians would give somewhat different points and therefore a somewhat different estimated line. This sampling variation is the reason the estimates need standard errors, tests and confidence intervals.

slides.title: The sample as the investigator sees it
paragraphs: The investigator sees only the 10 sampled points, without the rest of the population and without the true line of means.

The points rise from about 8 g at 31 cm to about 13 to 15 g at 42 to 46 cm, so heavier Martians tend to be taller. The points do not fall exactly on a line because individual weights scatter about the mean weight at each height.
The task is to choose the single straight line that best represents these points, and then to decide how precisely that line estimates the population line of means.

slides.title: Which line is best?
paragraphs: Four candidate lines are drawn through the sample. Lines I and II are poor because they lie far from most of the points. Lines III and IV both pass close to the data, so a precise rule is needed to choose between them.
The best line is defined as the line that minimizes the total variability between the data and the line.

The variability is measured by the vertical distances from each point to the line, because the line is meant to predict y from x. Squaring these distances before adding them makes positive and negative deviations both count and gives large misses extra weight.

slides.title: Gauss and the least-squares criterion
paragraphs: The least-squares idea is attributed to Gauss. The most probable values of the unknown quantities are those for which the sum of squared differences between the observed and computed values, weighted by their precision, is a minimum.

For simple regression the unknown quantities are the intercept and slope, the observed values are the measured y values, and the computed values are the heights of the line at each x. All points have equal precision, so the weights are equal.
Choosing a and b to make the sum of squared vertical deviations as small as possible gives the least-squares regression line.

slides.title: The least-squares regression line
paragraphs: Each observation is modeled as the line of means plus an error: \(y_i=\alpha+\beta x_i+e_i\). The error \(e_i\) is the vertical distance of that point from the line.
The sample line is written \(\hat y_i=a+bx_i\), where \(\hat y_i\) is the predicted value at \(x_i\). The residual \(y_i-\hat y_i\) is the vertical deviation drawn for each point in the figure.
The sum of squared errors is \(SS=\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2=\sum(y_i-(a+bx_i))^2\). Least squares chooses the a and b that make this sum as small as possible.
slides.symbols: \(y_i\) (observed value), \(x_i\) (independent variable), \(e_i\) (error), \(\hat y_i\) (predicted value on the sample line), \(a,b\) (sample intercept and slope), \(SS\) (sum of squared errors).

slides.title: Setting up the minimization
paragraphs: The data are n pairs \((x_i,y_i)\), one measurement of the independent and dependent variable for each subject.
The regression line \(\hat y=a+bx\) is the sample estimate of the population line \(\mu_{y|x}=\alpha+\beta x\): \(\hat y\) estimates \(\mu_{y|x}\), a estimates \(\alpha\), and b estimates \(\beta\).
SS depends on the two unknowns a and b. At the minimum, the partial derivative of SS with respect to each unknown equals zero, which gives two equations for the two unknowns.
slides.symbols: \((x_i,y_i)\) (paired measurements), \(\hat y\) (estimate of \(\mu_{y|x}\)), \(a,b\) (estimates of \(\alpha,\beta\)), \(SS\) (sum of squared errors).

slides.title: The normal equations and the intercept
paragraphs: Differentiating SS gives \(-2\sum(y_i-(a+bx_i))=0\) for a and \(-2\sum(y_i-(a+bx_i))x_i=0\) for b. Rearranging so a and b sit on the same side gives equations (1) and (2).
Equation (1) is \(\sum y_i=na+b\sum x_i\). Equation (2) is \(\sum x_iy_i=a\sum x_i+b\sum x_i^2\). These are two linear equations in the two unknowns.
Dividing equation (1) by n gives equation (3), \(a=\bar y-b\bar x\). The least-squares line therefore always passes through the point of means \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
slides.symbols: \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(a,b\) (least-squares intercept and slope).

slides.title: Closed-form least-squares slope and intercept
paragraphs: Substituting equation (3) into equation (2) and solving gives the slope \(b=\frac{n\sum x_iy_i-\sum x_i\sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2}\).
Substituting b back into equation (1) gives the intercept \(a=\frac{\sum y_i\sum x_i^2-\sum x_i\sum x_iy_i}{n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2}\). Both formulas share the same denominator.
Both coefficients need only five numbers: n, \(\sum x_i\), \(\sum y_i\), \(\sum x_i^2\) and \(\sum x_iy_i\). In practice b is calculated first and a follows from \(a=\bar y-b\bar x\).
equations: b=\frac{n\sum x_iy_i-\sum x_i\sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2}
a=\frac{\sum y_i\sum x_i^2-\sum x_i\sum x_iy_i}{n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2}
slides.symbols: \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\sum x_i,\sum y_i\) (sums of x and y), \(\sum x_i^2\) (sum of squared x), \(\sum x_iy_i\) (sum of cross-products).

slides.title: Computing the Martian regression line
paragraphs: Table 8-1 lists the 10 sampled heights and weights with \(x^2\) and \(xy\) for each Martian. The column totals are \(\sum x=369\) cm, \(\sum y=103.8\) g, \(\sum x^2=13{,}841\) cm² and \(\sum xy=3{,}930.1\) g·cm.
Rounded as on the slide, the regression line is \(\hat y=-6.0+0.44x\). It is close to, but not the same as, the population line of means \(\mu_{y|x}=-8+0.5x\), because it comes from one sample of 10.
slides.symbols: \(x\) (height, cm), \(y\) (weight, g), \(a\) (intercept, g), \(b\) (slope, g/cm), \(\hat y\) (predicted mean weight, g).

slides.title: The regression line estimates the line of means
paragraphs: The figure overlays the sample regression line \(\hat y=-6.0+0.44x\) on the true line of means \(\mu_{y|x}=-8+0.5x\). The two lines nearly coincide over the range of the data.
The regression line is an estimate of the line of means. Its intercept a estimates \(\alpha\) and its slope b estimates \(\beta\), and both carry sampling error.
A full description of the population also needs the spread about the line, \(\sigma_{y|x}=1\) g. The sample must provide an estimate of that spread as well.
slides.symbols: \(\mu_{y|x}\) (true line of means), \(\hat y\) (sample regression line), \(\sigma_{y|x}\) (true SD about the line).

slides.title: From population to sample line
paragraphs: The left panel shows the 200 Martians with the 10 sampled members filled in. The right panel shows only the sample, its regression line, and the true line of means.
The circled figure label gives the population values of the line of means: intercept \(-8.0\) g and slope 0.50 g/cm. The regression values are \(a=-6.0\) g and \(b=0.44\) g/cm.
The differences between a and \(\alpha\) and between b and \(\beta\) come only from which 10 Martians happened to be sampled. Standard errors quantify how large such differences typically are.

slides.title: Standard error of the estimate, s_y|x
paragraphs: The spread of population members about the line of means, \(\sigma_{y|x}\), is estimated from the residuals: \(s_{y|x}^2=\frac{1}{n-2}\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\).

The denominator is \(n-2\), not n or \(n-1\), because two quantities, a and b, were estimated from the same data before the residuals were formed. This also makes the degrees of freedom for regression \(\nu=n-2\).

An equivalent form uses the sample SDs of x and y: \(s_{y|x}=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n-2}(s_y^2-b^2s_x^2)}\). The quantity \(s_{y|x}\) is called the standard error of the estimate, and R reports it as the residual standard error.
slides.symbols: \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate), \(\hat y_i\) (predicted value), \(n\) (number of pairs), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs of x and y), \(b\) (slope).

slides.title: s_y|x for the 10 Martians
paragraphs: For the sample, \(s_x=5.0\) cm, \(s_y=2.4\) g, \(b=0.44\) g/cm and \(n=10\).
The shortcut gives \(s_{y|x}=\sqrt{\frac{9}{8}[2.4^2-0.44^2(5.0^2)]}=\sqrt{\frac98(5.76-4.84)}=1.02\) g. The subtraction removes the part of the y variance explained by the line.
The estimate 1.02 g is close to the true \(\sigma_{y|x}=1\) g. The shortcut is sensitive to rounding because it subtracts two similar numbers; the unrounded data give 0.964 g.
slides.symbols: \(s_x\) (SD of height, cm), \(s_y\) (SD of weight, g), \(b\) (slope, g/cm), \(s_{y|x}\) (estimate of \(\sigma_{y|x}\), g).

slides.title: Standard errors of the intercept and slope
paragraphs: The standard error of the slope is \(s_b=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}}\frac{s_{y|x}}{s_x}\). The slope is estimated more precisely when the scatter about the line is small, when n is large, and when the x values are spread widely.

The standard error of the intercept is \(s_a=s_{y|x}\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{\bar x^2}{(n-1)s_x^2}}\). The intercept is the predicted value at \(x=0\), so it becomes less precise as \(\bar x\) lies farther from zero.

For the Martians the slide reports \(s_a=2.6\) g and \(s_b=0.064\) g/cm. Substituting \(s_{y|x}=1.02\), \(\bar x=36.9\) and \(s_x=5.0\) into the formulas gives 2.53 g and 0.068 g/cm. The printed 0.064 g/cm matches the value from the unrounded data (0.0643 g/cm), for which \(s_a=2.39\) g.
slides.symbols: \(s_a\) (standard error of a), \(s_b\) (standard error of b), \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate), \(\bar x\) (mean of x), \(s_x\) (SD of x), \(n\) (number of pairs).

slides.title: Testing the significance of the trend
paragraphs: Every t statistic in the course has the same form: parameter estimate minus the true population value, divided by the standard error of the estimate. For the slope this is \(t=(b-\beta)/s_b\).
The question whether the variables are related becomes \(H_0:\beta=0\). Under this null, \(t=b/s_b\) with \(\nu=n-2\) degrees of freedom.
Reject \(H_0\) when \(|t|>t_\alpha(\nu)\) from the two-tailed t table. The left scatter has a clear slope; the right scatter has a nearly flat line, which gives a small t and no evidence of a trend.
slides.symbols: \(b\) (sample slope), \(\beta\) (population slope), \(s_b\) (standard error of b), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

hypotheses.nullWords: The slope of the population line of means is zero, so the mean of the dependent variable does not change linearly with the independent variable.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The slope of the population line of means is not zero, so the mean of the dependent variable changes linearly with the independent variable.

slides.title: The Martian trend test
paragraphs: The null hypothesis is that there is no relationship between height and weight in Martians, \(\beta=0\). The sample gives \(b=0.44\) g/cm with \(s_b=0.064\) g/cm.
The test statistic is \(t=0.44/0.064=6.875\) with \(\nu=10-2=8\). The printed two-tailed table gives \(t_{0.001}(8)=5.041\); the slide writes 5.401, which does not change the decision.
Because \(6.875>5.041\), the null hypothesis is rejected with \(P<0.001\). Martian weight increases with height.
slides.symbols: \(b\) (slope, g/cm), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope, g/cm), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

slides.title: Confidence intervals for the slope and intercept
paragraphs: The same t statement that gives the test also gives an interval. The \((1-\alpha)100\%\) confidence interval for the slope is \(b-t_\alpha(\nu)s_b<\beta<b+t_\alpha(\nu)s_b\).
The interval for the intercept of the line of means is \(a-t_\alpha(\nu)s_a<\alpha_{LOM}<a+t_\alpha(\nu)s_a\). The subscript LOM separates this intercept from the significance level \(\alpha\).
Both intervals use \(\nu=n-2\). If the interval for \(\beta\) excludes zero, the slope test rejects \(H_0:\beta=0\) at the matching level.
slides.symbols: \(\beta\) (population slope), \(\alpha_{LOM}\) (population intercept of the line of means), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value), \(s_a,s_b\) (standard errors).

slides.title: Confidence interval for the line of means
paragraphs: The predicted value \(\hat y=a+bx\) estimates the mean of y at a chosen x. Its standard error is \(s_{\hat y}=s_{y|x}\sqrt{\frac1n+\frac{(x-\bar x)^2}{(n-1)s_x^2}}\).

The standard error depends on x. It is smallest at \(x=\bar x\) and grows as x moves away from the mean, so the confidence band around the regression line is narrowest in the middle and flares out at both ends.

The interval is \(\hat y-t_\alpha(
u)s_{\hat y}<\mu_{y|x}<\hat y+t_\alpha(
u)s_{\hat y}\) with \(
u=n-2\). The figure marks the 95% interval for the mean weight of Martians 40 cm tall (the figure text says height, but the interval is on the weight axis).
slides.symbols: \(\hat y\) (predicted mean at x), \(s_{\hat y}\) (standard error of \(\hat y\)), \(\mu_{y|x}\) (true mean of y at x), \(x\) (chosen value), \(\bar x\) (mean of x), \(s_x\) (SD of x).

slides.title: Confidence interval for a single observation
paragraphs: A new individual at x differs from the line of means by its own random scatter, and the line itself is uncertain. The two variances add: \(s_{Y_{new}}=\sqrt{s_{y|x}^2+s_{\hat y}^2}=s_{y|x}\sqrt{1+\frac1n+\frac{(x-\bar x)^2}{(n-1)s_x^2}}\).

The interval is \(\hat y-t_\alpha(
u)s_{Y_{new}}<y<\hat y+t_\alpha(
u)s_{Y_{new}}\) with \(
u=n-2\). It includes uncertainty from variation in the population and uncertainty in the estimate of the true line of means.

Because of the extra 1 under the root, this interval is always wider than the interval for the mean at the same x, and it does not shrink to zero as n grows. The figure marks the 95% interval for the weight of an individual Martian 40 cm tall (the figure text again says height).
slides.symbols: \(s_{Y_{new}}\) (standard error for one new observation), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(s_{\hat y}\) (SE of the predicted mean), \(y\) (a single new observation at x).

slides.title: Comparing the slopes of two regression lines
paragraphs: Two regression lines are compared with \(t=\frac{b_1-b_2}{s_{b_1-b_2}}\), the difference of the slopes divided by the standard error of that difference, with \(\nu=n_1+n_2-4\) because each line uses two estimated coefficients.
When both lines have the same number of points, \(s_{b_1-b_2}=\sqrt{s_{b_1}^2+s_{b_2}^2}\), with each \(s_b=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n-1}}\frac{s_{y|x}}{s_x}\).

When the numbers differ, the scatter about the two lines is pooled, \(s_{y|x_p}^2=\frac{(n_1-2)s_{y|x_1}^2+(n_2-2)s_{y|x_2}^2}{n_1+n_2-4}\), and \(s_{b_1-b_2}=\sqrt{\frac{s_{y|x_p}^2}{(n_1-1)s_{x_1}^2}+\frac{s_{y|x_p}^2}{(n_2-1)s_{x_2}^2}}\). Reject \(H_0\) when \(|t|>t_\alpha(\nu)\); a corresponding test compares the intercepts.
slides.symbols: \(b_1,b_2\) (sample slopes), \(s_{b_1-b_2}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(s_{y|x_p}^2\) (pooled variance about the two lines), \(n_1,n_2\) (numbers of points), \(s_{x_1},s_{x_2}\) (SDs of x in each group).

hypotheses.nullWords: The two populations have lines of means with the same slope.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The slopes of the two populations' lines of means differ.

slides.title: Plutonian height and weight data
paragraphs: The example records height in inches (x) and weight in pounds (y) for 18 male and 18 female Plutonians, so \(n_M=n_F=18\).
Each sex is a separate sample, and each gives its own regression of weight on height.
Because the two samples are the same size, the equal-n formula for the standard error of the slope difference applies when the two lines are compared.

slides.title: Exploratory plots of the Plutonian data
paragraphs: Plotting the data before any test shows the form of the relationship. In males, weight rises closely and nearly linearly with height between 62 and 73 inches.
In females the points also rise with height, from 56 to 71 inches, but with much more scatter about any straight line.
On common axes, males are about 70 to 80 lb heavier than females at the heights where both groups overlap. Whether the rate of increase per inch differs between the sexes is a question about slopes.

slides.title: Three questions for the Plutonian data
paragraphs: The first two questions ask whether weight and height are significantly related within males and within females. Each is answered by a separate test of \(H_0:\beta=0\).
The third question applies only if both relationships are significant: whether the male relationship differs from the female one, divided into a comparison of slopes and a comparison of intercepts.
The plan is therefore to fit a regression for each sex, test each slope against zero, and then compare the two slopes with the two-line t test using \(\nu=n_1+n_2-4\).

slides.title: Question 1 in R: the males
paragraphs: The analysis for males fits the regression line of weight on height and tests whether the slope of the line of means differs from zero.
The R code keeps only the male rows with subset(mydata, Sex=='M'), fits the model with lm(formula = Weight.lbs ~ Height.in, data = males), and prints the results with summary().
In the formula, the variable on the left of ~ is the dependent variable (weight) and the variable on the right is the independent variable (height).

slides.title: Reading the lm() summary for males
paragraphs: The Estimate column gives the intercept \(a=-4.2329\) lb and the slope \(b=3.2833\) lb/in, so \(\hat y=-4.2329+3.2833x\). The Std. Error column gives \(s_a=13.7901\) and \(s_b=0.2041\).

The t value for the slope is \(3.2833/0.2041=16.088\), and Pr(>|t|) is \(2.66\times10^{-11}\) for the two-sided test of \(\beta=0\). The residual standard error is \(s_{y|x}=2.711\) lb on \(18-2=16\) degrees of freedom.

The decision is to reject \(H_0:\beta=0\) with P approximately 0: weight increases with height in male Plutonians. Multiple R-squared, 0.9418, is the square of the correlation coefficient, and the F statistic 258.8 equals \(t^2\) for simple regression.
slides.symbols: \(a\) (intercept, lb), \(b\) (slope, lb/in), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error, lb).

hypotheses.nullWords: The slope of the population line of means is zero, so the mean of the dependent variable does not change linearly with the independent variable.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The slope of the population line of means is not zero, so the mean of the dependent variable changes linearly with the independent variable.

slides.title: Male exercise: errors, intervals, r and predictions
paragraphs: The fitted line passes through the male data with little scatter. Since the relationship is significant, the follow-up questions ask for the standard errors and 95% intervals of \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), the correlation coefficient, the mean weight at 68 inches, and the 95% intervals for that mean and for one male.
In this notation \(b_0\) is the intercept a and \(b_1\) is the slope b. The standard errors are read from the lm() output, and the intervals use \(t_{0.05}(16)=2.120\).

The mean weight at 68 inches is \(\hat y=-4.2329+3.2833(68)=219.03\) lb. Its interval uses \(s_{\hat y}\), and the interval for one male uses the larger \(s_{Y_{new}}\), both evaluated with \(\bar x=67.5\) in and \(s_x=3.222\) in from the data table.

slides.title: Question 2 in R: the females
paragraphs: The female analysis repeats the male steps on the female rows: subset(mydata, Sex=='F'), then lm(formula = Weight.lbs ~ Height.in, data = females), then summary().
The same model formula is used, so the output can be compared line by line with the male output.
The aim is again to find the regression line and to test whether the slope of the female line of means differs from zero.

slides.title: Reading the lm() summary for females
paragraphs: The female line is \(\hat y=6.8349+2.0290x\), with \(s_a=29.8197\) and \(s_b=0.4708\). The residual standard error is \(s_{y|x}=7.491\) lb on 16 degrees of freedom, almost three times the male value.
Multiple R-squared is 0.5372, so \(r=\sqrt{0.5372}=0.733\). The female relationship is significant but weaker than the male relationship, matching the wider scatter seen in the exploratory plot.
slides.symbols: \(a\) (intercept, lb), \(b\) (slope, lb/in), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error, lb).

hypotheses.nullWords: The slope of the population line of means is zero, so the mean of the dependent variable does not change linearly with the independent variable.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The slope of the population line of means is not zero, so the mean of the dependent variable changes linearly with the independent variable.

slides.title: Female exercise: errors, intervals, r and predictions
paragraphs: The female follow-up repeats the male questions: standard errors and 95% intervals for \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), the correlation, and the mean and individual predictions at 68 inches.

With \(t_{0.05}(16)=2.120\), the slope interval is \(2.0290\pm2.120(0.4708)\), about 1.03 to 3.03 lb/in, which excludes zero. The intercept interval is very wide because \(x=0\) lies far from the data.

The predicted mean weight at 68 inches is \(6.8349+2.0290(68)=144.81\) lb. Since 68 inches is about 4.8 inches above the female mean height of 63.2 inches, \(s_{\hat y}\) is larger relative to \(s_{y|x}\) than it is for males at the same height.

slides.title: Question 3: are the male and female lines different?
paragraphs: The two fitted lines are \(\hat y=-4.2329+3.2833x\) for males and \(\hat y=6.8349+2.0290x\) for females. Both slopes are significantly different from zero, so the slopes can be compared.
Because \(2.444>t_{0.05}(32)=2.037\) but \(2.444<t_{0.02}(32)=2.449\), the slopes differ with \(0.02<P<0.05\). Male weight rises faster with height than female weight.
slides.symbols: \(b_1,b_2\) (male and female slopes), \(s_{b_1},s_{b_2}\) (their standard errors), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

slides.title: Correlation: strength of a relationship
paragraphs: The correlation coefficient r is a number between \(-1\) and \(+1\) that quantifies the strength of the relationship between two variables.

The closer the magnitude of r is to 1, the stronger the relationship and the less scatter about a straight line. The panels show \(r=+1\) (points exactly on a rising line), \(r=-1\) (exactly on a falling line), and \(r=+0.8\) (a rising trend with scatter).
A value near zero indicates a weak linear relationship, as in the round cloud with \(r=0\). The sign of r gives the direction of the relationship and the magnitude gives its strength.
slides.symbols: \(r\) (Pearson correlation coefficient).

slides.title: Correlation versus linear regression
paragraphs: Linear regression estimates how, on average, a dependent variable changes as an independent variable changes. It also estimates the variability of the dependent variable about the line of means.
The correlation coefficient quantifies the strength of association between two variables and does not require one variable to depend on the other.

For the same data, the regression of weight on height and the regression of height on weight are different lines, because each minimizes vertical deviations in its own dependent variable. The correlation coefficient is the same in either direction.

slides.title: The Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient
paragraphs: The Pearson coefficient is \(r=\frac{\sum(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2}}\). The numerator is the sum of cross-products of deviations from the means, which is positive when large x values go with large y values.
It is linked to the slope by \(r=\frac{\sqrt{\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2}}{\sqrt{\sum(y_i-\bar y)^2}}\cdot b\), so r and b always have the same sign and r = 0 exactly when b = 0.
An r close to +1 means the variables increase together, close to \(-1\) means they have an inverse relationship, and close to 0 means there is no linear relationship.
slides.symbols: \(r\) (correlation coefficient), \(x_i,y_i\) (paired observations), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(b\) (regression slope of y on x).

slides.title: Martian correlation coefficient
paragraphs: Table 8-3 lists each Martian's deviations from the mean height (36.9 cm) and mean weight (10.38 g), their products and their squares.
The column totals are \(\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)=99.9\) g·cm, \(\sum(x-\bar x)^2=224.9\) cm² and \(\sum(y-\bar y)^2=51.8\) g².
The coefficient is \(r=\frac{99.9}{\sqrt{(224.9)(51.8)}}=0.925\). The units cancel, and the value close to 1 shows a strong positive linear relationship between Martian height and weight.
equations: r=\frac{\sum(x-\bar x)(y-\bar y)}{\sqrt{\sum(x-\bar x)^2\sum(y-\bar y)^2}}=\frac{99.9\text{ g}\cdot\text{cm}}{\sqrt{(224.9\text{ cm}^2)(51.8\text{ g}^2)}}=0.925
slides.symbols: \(r\) (correlation coefficient), \(\bar x\) (mean height, cm), \(\bar y\) (mean weight, g).

slides.title: Testing whether the correlation is zero
paragraphs: The null hypothesis is that there is no linear relationship between the two variables in the population, written on the slide as r = 0.
The test statistic is \(t=r\sqrt{\frac{n-2}{1-r^2}}\) with \(\nu=n-2\). It equals the slope statistic \(b/s_b\) for the same data, so the correlation test and the slope test reach the same decision.
Reject \(H_0\) with \(P<\alpha\) when \(|t|>t_{crit}=t_\alpha(\nu)\) from the two-tailed t table.
slides.symbols: \(r\) (sample correlation coefficient), \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

slides.title: The lm() function and related R functions
paragraphs: The R call results <- lm(formula = Y ~ X, data = dataname) fits the simple linear regression of Y on X; lm stands for linear model. print(results) shows the coefficients and summary(results) shows the full table with standard errors, t values, P values and the residual standard error.

coefficients(results) or coef(results) returns a and b; confint(results, level = 0.95) returns the confidence intervals for the intercept and slope; residuals(results) returns \(y_i-\hat y_i\); and predict(results, ...) returns fitted values and, with options, intervals at chosen x values.
plot() displays the data against the regression line. cor(x = dataname$X, y = dataname$Y) returns r, and cor.test(...) performs the t test of zero correlation.

slides.title: lm() example 1: reproducing the Martian results
paragraphs: The first R exercise reproduces the by-hand Martian results: the slope and intercept, the residual standard error, the standard errors of the coefficients, the significance of the trend, and the 95% intervals for the line of means and for an individual weight at 40 cm.

R works with unrounded numbers, so its residual standard error (0.964 g) differs from the by-hand 1.02 g, which came from rounded summary values. The exercise notes that small rounding errors compounded in the slide calculation.

slides.title: lm() example 2: LVEF and age in myocarditis
paragraphs: The second exercise uses patients with acute dilated cardiomyopathy resulting from myocarditis, from Dec and colleagues (1985) in the New England Journal of Medicine, and examines the relationship between left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and age.

The questions ask for the slope and intercept of the regression of LVEF on age, whether the relationship is significant, the average LVEF of a 45-year-old patient, the standard errors and 95% intervals of the slope and intercept, the correlation coefficient, and whether it differs from zero.

methods.title: Least-squares regression line → slope b and intercept a
methods.trigger: Paired measurements of two variables (or their sums Σx, Σy, Σx², Σxy) are given and the question asks for the regression line of the dependent variable on the independent variable.
formula: b=\frac{n\sum x_iy_i-\sum x_i\sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2}
methods.shortcut: Compute \(S_{xx}=\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2/n\) and \(S_{xy}=\sum xy-\sum x\sum y/n\); then \(b=S_{xy}/S_{xx}\) and \(a=\bar y-b\bar x\). Carry b unrounded into a.
paragraphs: The population model is a line of means \(\mu_{y|x}=\alpha+\beta x\) with Normal scatter of constant SD \(\sigma_{y|x}\) at every x. A sample line \(\hat y=a+bx\) estimates it.

Least squares chooses a and b to minimize \(\sum(y_i-\hat y_i)^2\), the sum of squared vertical deviations. Setting both partial derivatives to zero gives the closed-form slope and the intercept \(a=\bar y-b\bar x\), so the line passes through \((\bar x,\bar y)\).
The slope has units of y per unit x and gives the estimated change in the mean of y for a one-unit increase in x. The intercept is the predicted mean at x = 0, which may lie far outside the data.
methods.symbols: \(n\) (number of pairs), \(x_i,y_i\) (paired observations), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(a,b\) (sample intercept and slope), \(\hat y\) (predicted mean).

methods.title: Scatter about the line → s_y|x, s_a and s_b
methods.trigger: The question asks for the residual (standard error of the estimate) SD about the regression line, or for the standard errors of the intercept and slope.
methods.shortcut: Note \((n-1)s_x^2=S_{xx}\), so \(s_b=s_{y|x}/\sqrt{S_{xx}}\). Keep full precision in the shortcut for \(s_{y|x}\), because it subtracts two similar numbers.
paragraphs: \(s_{y|x}\) estimates \(\sigma_{y|x}\), the spread of the population about the line of means. Its denominator is \(n-2\) because a and b were estimated first; R prints it as the residual standard error.

The slope's standard error shrinks with less scatter, more points, and a wider spread of x values. The intercept's standard error grows with \(\bar x^2\), because the intercept is an extrapolation to x = 0.
methods.symbols: \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs), \(b\) (slope), \(s_a,s_b\) (standard errors of a and b), \(\bar x\) (mean of x).

methods.title: Slope t test and CIs for β and α → significance of the trend
methods.trigger: The question asks whether there is a significant relationship (trend) between two variables, or asks for a confidence interval for the slope or intercept, by hand or from lm() output.
methods.shortcut: In lm() output, the slope row already gives b, s_b, t = b/s_b and the two-sided P; confint() gives both intervals.
paragraphs: The null \(H_0:\beta=0\) states that the mean of y does not change linearly with x. The statistic \(t=b/s_b\) is compared with the two-tailed cutoff \(t_\alpha(n-2)\); reject when \(|t|>t_\alpha(\nu)\) and report the P range from the bracketing columns.
The same t value builds the intervals \(b\pm t_\alpha(\nu)s_b\) and \(a\pm t_\alpha(\nu)s_a\). An interval for \(\beta\) that excludes zero agrees with rejecting \(H_0\) at the matching level.
methods.symbols: \(b,a\) (sample slope and intercept), \(s_b,s_a\) (their standard errors), \(\beta\) (population slope), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

methods.title: Prediction at x → CI for the line of means vs CI for one observation
methods.trigger: The question asks for the mean of y at a given x with its confidence interval, or for the range expected for a single new individual at that x.
methods.shortcut: Compute the bracket \(B=\frac1n+\frac{(x-\bar x)^2}{(n-1)s_x^2}\) once: \(s_{\hat y}=s_{y|x}\sqrt B\) and \(s_{Y_{new}}=s_{y|x}\sqrt{1+B}\).
paragraphs: The mean interval describes where the line of means lies at x; it is narrowest at \(x=\bar x\) and shrinks as n grows.
The observation interval adds the individual scatter \(s_{y|x}^2\), so it is always wider and never shrinks below about \(\pm t\,s_{y|x}\). Both use \(\nu=n-2\).
methods.symbols: \(\hat y\) (predicted mean at x), \(s_{\hat y}\) (SE of the predicted mean), \(s_{Y_{new}}\) (SE for one new observation), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(\bar x,s_x\) (mean and SD of x).

methods.title: Two regression lines → t test for a difference in slopes
methods.trigger: Two groups each have their own regression of y on x, and the question asks whether the slopes (or intercepts) differ.
methods.shortcut: With equal group sizes, read \(s_{b_1}\) and \(s_{b_2}\) straight from the two lm() slope rows and combine them as \(\sqrt{s_{b_1}^2+s_{b_2}^2}\).
paragraphs: First confirm that each slope differs from zero; then test \(H_0:\beta_1=\beta_2\) with the difference of slopes over its standard error and \(\nu=n_1+n_2-4\).

With equal numbers of points the slide combines the two slope standard errors directly; with unequal numbers it pools the residual variances about both lines first. The corresponding intercept test replaces slopes and their SEs by intercepts and their SEs.
methods.symbols: \(b_1,b_2\) (sample slopes), \(s_{b_1},s_{b_2}\) (their SEs), \(s_{y|x_p}^2\) (pooled variance about the lines), \(n_1,n_2\) (group sizes), \(s_{x_1},s_{x_2}\) (SDs of x in each group).

methods.title: Pearson correlation r → strength of association and its t test
methods.trigger: The question asks how strongly two variables are associated, for the Pearson correlation coefficient, or whether the correlation differs from zero.
methods.shortcut: From lm() output, \(r=\pm\sqrt{R^2}\) with the sign of the slope, and the correlation t equals the slope t.
paragraphs: r lies between −1 and +1; its sign gives the direction and its magnitude the strength of the linear relationship. It does not require one variable to depend on the other and is unchanged when x and y are swapped.
The test of no linear relationship uses \(t=r\sqrt{(n-2)/(1-r^2)}\) with \(\nu=n-2\) and the two-tailed table, and it reaches the same decision as the slope test.
methods.symbols: \(r\) (Pearson correlation coefficient), \(x_i,y_i\) (paired observations), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (means), \(b\) (slope of y on x), \(n\) (number of pairs).

cases.symbols: \(x\) (dose, mg), \(y\) (taps per 10 s), \(S_{xx},S_{yy},S_{xy}\) (sums of squared and cross deviations), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(s_a,s_b\) (SEs of the coefficients), \(s_{\hat y},s_{Y_{new}}\) (SEs for the mean and for one volunteer), \(r\) (correlation).

steps.title: Calculate both means
steps.words: These are the coordinates of the point the regression line passes through.

steps.title: Calculate the deviation sums
steps.words: These equal Σ(x−x̄)², Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) and Σ(y−ȳ)².

steps.title: Calculate the slope
general: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}
steps.words: Equivalently b = S_xy/S_xx = 15336.4/338720. Tapping rate rises by about 0.045 taps per 10 s per mg.

steps.title: Calculate the intercept
steps.words: The line is ŷ = 50.80 + 0.04528x.

steps.title: Calculate the sample variances
steps.words: These feed the shortcut formula for s_y|x.

steps.title: Estimate the variance about the line of means
steps.words: This is the requested estimate of the variance of the line of means, in (taps/10 s)².

steps.title: Calculate the coefficient standard errors
steps.words: Note (n−1)s_x² = S_xx = 338720.

steps.title: Calculate t and bracket the missing table row
steps.words: Row 43 is not printed. Bracket it with rows 42 and 44 on PDF page 1 and use the conservative row-42 cutoff 2.018 (the two rows differ by only 0.003).

steps.title: Decide and give the P range
steps.words: t exceeds both bracketing 0.001 cutoffs, so the trend is significant with P < 0.001.

steps.title: Construct the 95% CI for the mean at 200 mg
steps.words: Using the row-44 value 2.015 would move the lower bound only to 58.3309.

steps.title: Construct the 95% CI for one volunteer at 200 mg
steps.words: The single-observation interval is much wider because it includes the person-to-person scatter.

steps.title: Calculate the correlation coefficient
steps.words: A moderate positive correlation. Its t statistic equals b/s_b, so the correlation test agrees with the slope test.

questions.stem: Using the column totals for the 10 Martians, what is the least-squares slope b?
questions.why: The slope is (10·3930.1 − 369·103.8)/(10·13841 − 369²) = 998.8/2249 = 0.4441 g/cm. The value 0.5 g/cm is the population slope, which the sample only estimates.
equations: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}

questions.stem: What is the least-squares intercept a for the Martian sample?
questions.why: With the unrounded slope, a = ȳ − b x̄ = 10.38 − 0.4441(36.9) = −6.008 g. Rounding b to 0.44 first gives −5.856 g, and adding instead of subtracting gives 26.77 g.

questions.stem: Using the slide's rounded values, what is the standard error of the estimate \(s_{y|x}\)?
questions.why: s_y|x = √[(9/8)(5.76 − 4.84)] = √1.035 = 1.017 g. Forgetting the root gives 1.035, dropping the 9/8 factor gives 0.959, and inverting it gives 0.904.

questions.stem: With \(s_{y|x}=1.017\) g and \(s_x=5.0\) cm, what is the standard error of the slope \(s_b\)?
questions.why: s_b = (1/√9)(1.017/5.0) = 0.0678 g/cm. Omitting 1/√(n−1) gives 0.2035, dividing by 9 instead of 3 gives 0.0226, and using s_x² gives 0.0136.

questions.stem: With \(s_{y|x}=1.017\) g, what is the standard error of the intercept \(s_a\) for the Martians?
questions.why: s_a = 1.017√(0.1 + 36.9²/(9·25)) = 1.017√6.1516 = 2.523 g. Dropping the x̄² term gives 0.322, skipping the root gives 6.258, and dropping 1/n gives 2.503.

questions.stem: What is the t statistic for testing \(H_0:\beta=0\) with b = 0.44 g/cm and \(s_b=0.064\) g/cm?
questions.why: t = b/s_b = 0.44/0.064 = 6.875. Using the population slope 0.5 in the numerator would give 7.813, which is not the null value.

questions.stem: Which printed two-tailed value is \(t_{0.001}(8)\) in the course t table?
questions.why: Row 8, column 0.001 prints 5.041. The slide writes 5.401, a transposition; 4.781 is row 9 and 3.355 is the 0.01 column.

questions.stem: What is the lower endpoint of the 95% confidence interval for the Martian slope β?
questions.why: 0.44 − 2.306(0.064) = 0.2924 g/cm with ν = 8. Using ν = 10 (2.228) gives 0.2974, using 1.96 gives 0.3146, and using the 0.001 cutoff gives 0.1174.

questions.stem: What is the standard error of the predicted mean weight \(s_{\hat y}\) at 40 cm?
questions.why: s_ŷ = 1.02√(0.1 + 3.1²/225) = 0.3853 g. Omitting the distance term gives 0.3226, and 1.0904 g is the SE for one new Martian.

questions.stem: What is the lower endpoint of the 95% CI for the mean weight of Martians 40 cm tall?
questions.why: 11.6 − 2.306(0.3853) = 10.711 g. The value 9.086 g is the lower bound for one Martian, 10.845 g uses 1.96, and 11.215 g subtracts only one SE.

questions.stem: From the Table 8-3 totals, what is the Martian correlation coefficient r?
questions.why: r = 99.9/√(224.9·51.8) = 0.9256. The value 0.8567 is r², 0.4442 is the slope b, and 1.929 divides by the y sum of squares alone.

questions.stem: Using \(r=0.9256\) and n = 10, what is the t statistic for testing zero correlation?
questions.why: t = r√[(n−2)/(1−r²)] = 0.9256√(8/0.1433) = 6.915. Using n instead of n−2 gives 7.731, omitting 1−r² gives 2.618, and using 1−r gives 9.595.

questions.stem: For male Plutonians, what is the lower endpoint of the 95% CI for the slope \(b_1\)?
questions.why: 3.2833 − 2.120(0.2041) = 2.851 lb/in with ν = 16. Using 1.96 gives 2.883, one SE gives 3.079, and the 0.001 cutoff gives 2.464.

questions.stem: What is the correlation coefficient for male Plutonian height and weight?
questions.why: r is the square root of multiple R-squared with the sign of the slope: √0.9418 = 0.9705. The adjusted R-squared is not used.

questions.stem: What is the predicted mean weight of a male Plutonian 68 inches tall?
questions.why: ŷ = −4.2329 + 3.2833(68) = 219.0315 lb. Omitting the intercept gives 223.2644; 217.3889 is the male mean weight (at 67.5 in); 144.8069 comes from the female line.

questions.stem: What is the lower endpoint of the 95% CI for the weight of one male Plutonian 68 inches tall?
questions.why: With s_Ynew = √(2.711² + 0.6471²) = 2.787 lb, the bound is 219.032 − 2.120(2.787) = 213.123 lb. Using s_y|x alone gives 213.284 and using 1.96 gives 213.569.

questions.stem: What is the standard error of the difference between the male and female slopes?
questions.why: With equal n, s = √(0.2041² + 0.4708²) = 0.5131 lb/in. Adding the SEs gives 0.6749, skipping the root gives 0.2633, and averaging the variances gives 0.3628.

questions.stem: What is the t statistic for comparing the male and female slopes?
questions.why: t = (3.2833 − 2.0290)/0.5131 = 2.444. Dividing by the sum of SEs gives 1.858, by the variance sum gives 4.764, and by the male SE alone gives 6.146.

questions.stem: For the female Plutonian line, what is the upper endpoint of the 95% CI for the slope?
questions.why: 2.0290 + 2.120(0.4708) = 3.027 lb/in with ν = 16. Using 1.96 gives 2.952, one SE gives 2.500, and the 0.001 cutoff gives 3.919.

questions.stem: Using the female line, what is the predicted mean weight of a female Plutonian 68 inches tall?
questions.why: ŷ = 6.8349 + 2.0290(68) = 144.8069 lb. Omitting the intercept gives 137.972, 135.1111 is the female mean weight, and 219.0315 comes from the male line.

questions.stem: From the given sums, what is the slope of tapping rate on caffeine dose?
questions.why: b = S_xy/S_xx = 15336.4/338720 = 0.04528. Inverting gives 22.09, dividing by the raw Σx² gives 0.0123, and Σxy/Σx² gives 0.3058.
equations: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}

questions.stem: What is the estimated variance about the line of means, \(s_{y|x}^2\), for the caffeine data?
questions.why: s²_y|x = (44/43)(33.169 − 15.782) = 17.792. Omitting 44/43 gives 17.388, 4.218 is the SD rather than the variance, and 33.169 is s_y².

questions.stem: What is the lower endpoint of the 95% CI for the mean tapping rate at 200 mg?
questions.why: ŷ = 59.855 and s_ŷ = 0.7564, so 59.855 − 2.018(0.7564) = 58.3286 with the bracketed ν = 43 cutoff. 51.207 is the one-volunteer bound, 59.099 subtracts one SE, and 58.373 uses 1.96.

questions.stem: What is the Pearson correlation between caffeine dose and tapping rate?
Why does \(s_{y|x}^2\) divide the residual sum of squares by \(n-2\)?
options: The x and y variables each lose one degree of freedom for their means.
Two coefficients, a and b, are estimated from the same data before the residuals are formed.
Dividing by n − 2 makes the variance larger so the test is always conservative.
The first and last points are not used when the residuals are formed.
questions.why: Fitting the line uses the data to estimate two parameters, which removes two degrees of freedom from the residuals; the same ν = n − 2 is used for the t tests.

questions.stem: Which line does the least-squares criterion select?
options: The line that minimizes the sum of perpendicular distances from the points to the line.
The line that passes through the largest number of observed points.
The line joining the points with the smallest and largest x values.
The line that minimizes the sum of squared vertical deviations of the points from the line.
questions.why: Least squares chooses a and b to make Σ(y − ŷ)² as small as possible, measuring the misses vertically in the dependent variable.

questions.stem: Which statement is NOT one of the population assumptions for linear regression?
options: The independent variable x must be Normally distributed.
The mean of y at each x lies on the straight line α + βx.
At each value of x, the values of y are Normally distributed.
The SD of y about the line of means is the same at every x.
questions.why: The assumptions concern y at each fixed x: linear means, Normal scatter, and constant σ_y|x. No distribution is assumed for x.

questions.stem: In R's summary() of an lm() fit, which line reports \(s_{y|x}\)?
options: Std. Error in the Height.in row
questions.why: s_y|x, the standard error of the estimate, is printed as the residual standard error, with n − 2 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Why is the CI for one new observation at x wider than the CI for the line of means at the same x?
options: It uses a larger critical t value with fewer degrees of freedom.
It is computed at the mean of x instead of at the chosen x.
It uses the slope's standard error in place of the residual standard error.
It adds the scatter of individuals about the line to the uncertainty in the estimated line.
questions.why: s_Ynew = √(s²_y|x + s²_ŷ): the extra s²_y|x term reflects individual variation, which remains even when the line is known exactly.

questions.stem: At which value of x is the standard error of the predicted mean \(s_{\hat y}\) smallest?
options: It is the same at every x
questions.why: The term (x − x̄)² vanishes at the mean of x, so the confidence band is narrowest there and widens toward both ends.

questions.stem: Two regression lines with \(n_1\) and \(n_2\) points are compared by their slopes. How many degrees of freedom does the t test use?
questions.why: Each line estimates two coefficients, so four degrees of freedom are used; for 18 males and 18 females ν = 32.

questions.stem: The regression of y on x and the regression of x on y are fitted to the same data. Which statement is true?
options: The two lines differ, but the correlation coefficient is the same.
The two lines are identical whenever r is positive.
The correlation coefficient changes sign when the variables are swapped.
Only the regression of y on x has a correlation coefficient.
questions.why: Each regression minimizes vertical deviations in its own dependent variable, so the lines differ; r is symmetric in x and y.

questions.stem: What does a correlation coefficient close to \(-1\) indicate?
options: No relationship between the two variables.
A strong inverse linear relationship: one variable decreases as the other increases.
A weak positive relationship with large scatter.
That y does not depend on x, so regression cannot be used.
questions.why: The sign gives the direction and the magnitude gives the strength; r near −1 means points lie close to a falling straight line.

questions.stem: In the lm() coefficient table, what does Pr(>|t|) in the slope row test?
options: Whether the residuals are Normally distributed.
Whether the intercept equals the slope.
Whether the slope equals the correlation coefficient.
The two-sided null hypothesis that the population slope β is zero.
questions.why: The slope's t value is b/s_b, and Pr(>|t|) is its two-sided P value under H0: β = 0 with n − 2 degrees of freedom.

questions.stem: Which R function returns the confidence intervals for the intercept and slope of a fitted lm() model?
questions.why: confint() gives the coefficient intervals a ± t s_a and b ± t s_b; predict() gives fitted values and prediction intervals.

questions.stem: For the same data, how does the t statistic for \(H_0\): zero correlation compare with the t statistic \(b/s_b\) for \(H_0:\beta=0\)?
options: The correlation t is always larger because it ignores the slope.
The correlation t uses n − 1 degrees of freedom instead of n − 2.
They are equal, so both tests reach the same decision.
They cannot be compared because r has no units.
questions.why: r√[(n−2)/(1−r²)] equals b/s_b algebraically, and both use ν = n − 2; the Martian data give 6.907 either way when unrounded.

questions.stem: In \(\hat y=a+bx\), what does each sample quantity estimate?
options: \(\hat y\) estimates \(\sigma_{y|x}\), a estimates \(\beta\), and b estimates \(\alpha\).
\(\hat y\) estimates a single observation exactly, with no error.
a and b are the population values, and \(\hat y\) is the sample mean of y.
\(\hat y\) estimates \(\mu_{y|x}\), a estimates \(\alpha\), and b estimates \(\beta\).
questions.why: The regression line is the sample estimate of the population line of means μ_y|x = α + βx.

questions.stem: When two regression lines have different numbers of points, how is the scatter about the lines combined?
questions.why: Each line's residual variance is weighted by its own n − 2 degrees of freedom, and the total is divided by n1 + n2 − 4.

questions.stem: The male Plutonian lm() output shows Multiple R-squared 0.9418 and a positive slope. What is r?
questions.why: In simple regression R-squared equals r², and r takes the sign of the slope.

questions.stem: Why is the Martian intercept so much less precise than the slope (\(s_a\approx2.5\) g versus \(s_b\approx0.07\) g/cm)?
options: The intercept is measured in grams, which always have larger errors than g/cm.
The intercept uses n − 1 degrees of freedom instead of n − 2.
The intercept is the prediction at x = 0, far from the mean height of 36.9 cm, so the \(\bar x^2\) term inflates \(s_a\).
The intercept ignores the scatter about the line.
questions.why: s_a = s_y|x√[1/n + x̄²/((n−1)s_x²)]; extrapolating 36.9 cm below the data makes the x̄² term dominate.

sourceNotes.text: The slide title reads "Sample data from Marian Population"; the data are the sample of 10 Martians.
The textbook figure (also on pages 16, 19, 20 and 22) labels the intercept of the line of means "μ = −8.0 g". The intercept of the line of means is α = −8.0 g; μ_y|x denotes the line itself.

s_y|x = 1.02 g comes from the rounded summaries s_x = 5.0 cm, s_y = 2.4 g and b = 0.44 g/cm (unrounded shortcut value 1.0173 g). From the ten raw observations the residual standard error is 0.9643 g, which is what R reports; slide 43 attributes the difference to rounding.

Substituting the slide's s_y|x = 1.02 g, x̄ = 36.9 cm and s_x = 5.0 cm gives s_b = 1.02/(3·5.0) = 0.068 g/cm and s_a = 2.53 g, not the printed 0.064 g/cm and 2.6 g. The unrounded data give s_b = 0.0643 g/cm and s_a = 2.392 g. The worked case shows the arithmetic from the formulas; the trend test (page 22) uses the printed 0.064 as given.

The slide gives t_0.001(8) = 5.401. The printed course t table (t_table.pdf, page 1, row 8, column 0.001) gives 5.041. The conclusion is unchanged because t = 6.875 exceeds either value. With unrounded b and s_b the statistic is 6.907.
The figure text reads "95% CI for mean height at 40 cm"; the interval marked is for mean weight at a height of 40 cm.
The figure text reads "95% CI for individual height at 40 cm"; the interval marked is for the weight of an individual Martian at a height of 40 cm.

The slide's equal-n rule gives s_b1−b2 = 0.5131 and t = 2.444. Applying the pooled formula from page 26 to the same data gives s_b1−b2 = 0.5524 and t = 2.271, because the two groups have different s_x. Both fall between t_0.05(32) = 2.037 and t_0.02(32) = 2.449, so the decision (0.02 < P < 0.05) is the same.
This page is headed "IV. Correlation", while the outline on page 1 and page 41 number Correlation as section V.

In Table 8-3 the (Y − Ȳ)² entries for the rows x = 35, 35 and 40 print as 0.3, 2.0 and 2.0. The deviations −0.78, −0.58 and 1.42 give 0.6, 0.3 and 2.0. The column total 51.8 is correct, so r = 0.925 is unaffected.
The slide writes the null hypothesis as r = 0. The hypothesis concerns the population correlation (often written ρ); r is the sample statistic used to test it.

The exercise cites Lecture Slides 14, 18, 19, 21, 23 and 24. In this PDF the matching pages are 15 (slope and intercept values), 18–19 (s_y|x), 20 (standard errors), 22 (trend test), 24 (CI for the line of means) and 25 (CI for one observation).
The citation line reads "312:885-890, 195."; the article is dated 1985 at the end of the author line. No data are printed on the slide, so this example has no worked case here.
